approach: Each term hides a factor of the one-second interval written as the bare number 1; restoring that factor shows the expression is dimensionally consistent.

steps.text: sₜ is the displacement during the t-th second, the interval between time t − 1 s and time t, found from the position formula s(τ) = uτ + ½aτ².
Expanding this difference and grouping terms gives every part of sₜ multiplied by a factor of the one-second interval, which the short form of the equation leaves unwritten.
steps.equation: sₜ = u(1 s) + ½a(1 s)(2t − 1 s)

steps.text: Check the dimension of each term: u(1 s) is a velocity times a time, a length; ½a(1 s)(2t − 1 s) is an acceleration times two time intervals, also a length.
steps.why_this_step: Once both time intervals are written out, every term on the right has the dimension of length, matching sₜ.

steps.text: Writing the 1 s factors as the bare number 1, as the short form does, gives sₜ = u + at − ½a; the formula looks unbalanced only because that unit has been dropped, not because it is wrong.
steps.equation: sₜ = u + at − ½a, with the 1 s factors suppressed

final_answer.value: The 1 s interval in each term is written as the bare number 1. Restoring it gives sₜ = u(1 s) + ½a(1 s)(2t − 1 s), where every term is a length, so the equation is dimensionally consistent once the suppressed unit is put back.

common_mistakes.text: Concluding the relation is dimensionally wrong outright, instead of noticing that its second and third terms carry a suppressed factor of 1 s that restores their dimension of length.
